To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the African swine fever (ASF) epizootic is spreading across the European Union (EU), and wild boars are playing an increasing role in the epidemiology.

the epizootic was caused by the introduction of ASF virus into the wild boar population in the eastern part of the EU, and the virus spread through the environment, including the wild boar–environment transmission cycle.
the wild boar–environment transmission cycle is a key factor in the current African swine fever outbreak and that this cycle should be considered in the development of new control strategies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of wild boar–habit epidemiologic cycle in African swine fever.
the epidemiology of African swine fever virus in Europe and the role of wild boar as a reservoir of this virus.
the identification of a novel epidemiologic cycle for African swine fever virus transmission in wild boar and habitat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
African swine fever is a zoonosis, and that the disease is transmitted by the tick Ornithodoros erraticus, which is found in pigsties and pig farms, and by the wild boar.
the African swine fever virus (ASFV) is not transmissible by the air route, but that transmission can occur through the ingestion of contaminated food, water, and soil.

African swine fever virus can be transmitted to susceptible pigs by wild boar in the field, and that the virus can survive in the environment for long periods, even under unfavorable environmental conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

wild boar–habitats are the most likely reservoirs of African swine fever virus in Europe, that wild boar are the main source for virus reintroduction, and that the wild boar–pig interface is the main transmission cycle.
the wild boar–environment cycle is an important transmission pathway for African swine fever and that the epizootic is likely to persist until control measures are implemented.

the virus can be transmitted by wild boar to susceptible domestic pigs in the presence of susceptible wild boar and susceptible domestic pigs, and in the absence of domestic pigs, the virus can be maintained by the transmission cycle between susceptible wild boar.
The main takeaway from our work is that
wild boar–environment transmission can be the dominant mode in some areas and can explain the persistence of the disease in some areas.
the wild boar–habitats cycle is a significant component in the African swine fever epidemiology and is responsible for the long-term persistence of the virus and for the maintenance of endemicity.
